::: {.notes}
*⏱ 0:45 · Tanya*

**Tanya:** This is where I come in. In 2024, Jadey reached out to me for help on the next evolution of the project - building a Shiny app to deliver Quarto reports. We previously connected years before via the Twitterverse and R-Ladies community- I was ecstatic to get a chance to work with her.

The pitch was straight forward, build an intuitive interface to let non technical people customize and run their own reports. Together we built the Shiny app, Dirt Data Reports, which sits on top of the {soils} package and the parameterized Quarto template. Users didn’t need to know Quarto let alone how to spell Quarto. All they had to do was drop in their data, enter their project-specific information, and click “Build Reports”.

No R. No terminal. Let’s take a sneak peek at how it works.

**[next slide: the recorded demo]**
:::

*⏱ 1:30–2:00 · Tanya, narrating over the recording*

**[press space or click the video to play; the deck's arrow keys still work while it plays. Cut: upload → parameters → render → download.]**

**Tanya (over the video):** Drag in the sample data. Pick the farmer, pick the year, pick the format. Hit render. That's `{soils}` doing the work underneath, the same functions Jadey showed you. Preview on the right. Download the PDF. That's the whole workflow for a the person supporting the farmers.

The important thing isn't that this is a Shiny app. It's that the person using it never has to know there's a package, a template, or Quarto underneath. They open the bag and eat the cookie.

**[hand-off to Jadey on the next slide]**

## What We Saw {#app-aftermath}

{{< rings lit=3 class="rings--crumb" >}}

::: {.lede}
Real users showed us what worked, and what didn't.
:::

::: {.fill .fill--center}
```{=html}
<div class="flow">
  <div class="node card card--l3">
    <p class="emphasis">&plus; Positive signal</p>
    <p class="muted">The app saved time and effort.</p>
  </div>
  <div class="arrow"> </div>
  <div class="node card card--l3">
    <p class="emphasis">&minus; Negative signal</p>
    <p class="muted">Different projects surfaced new needs.</p>
  </div>
</div>
```
:::

::: {.notes}
*⏱ 0:45 · Jadey*

**Jadey:** In September 2025, we released Dirt Data Reports into the universe, but our story doesn’t stop there. We took inventory on what worked and what didn’t and created a feedback loop with users.

We started getting some really useful signals. 

**On the positive side** - it was clear that organizations were using the app and saving real time and effort by automating their reports.

**But there was also a negative signal** - once people started using it for different projects, they started pushing beyond the original assumptions and scope we had designed for. They needed more customization in some areas and more guardrails in others. This meant baking in more features to match their needs.
:::

. . .
